name: Nice Cote d'Azur
brief: A strip of usable airspace between the Maritime Alps and the sea. The mountains start a few miles inland and climb hard -- there is a minimum safe altitude over them that is higher than the level you want to be at on the approach -- so almost all vectoring happens over the water to the south. Arrivals are brought down the coast and turned in from the sea rather than from behind the field, which makes the base leg short and the intercept unforgiving. Two close parallel runways handle it. The sea breeze turns through the day and the field turns round with it, so the direction you started in is not necessarily the one you finish in.

provenance.notes: The aerodrome reference point, the runway designators and bearings, and the field elevation are real to the best of the author knowledge. EVERYTHING ELSE IS CONSTRUCTED: the entry fixes and their names, the airspace boundary, the terrain and noise areas and the traffic mix are invented to give the sector a shape to control, and are NOT taken from any AIP. Do not use for anything but this game. Contrast egll.json, whose positions are surveyed. Runway thresholds are derived from the strip: a centre on the reference point, the published bearing, and the published length, with the two ends half a length either side. Only the aerodrome VOR carries a frequency; the entry gates are plain waypoints. The two parallels are opened out to about seven hundred metres rather than the real three hundred, so that they read as two runways at scope range. Terrain is drawn as nested contour bands, each the ground above a height, with the summits at their real positions and heights; the outlines between them are shaped by hand to sit right against the coast and are not surveyed. The airspace volumes are CONSTRUCTED and are not from any AIP or sector file: a control zone shaped round the runway, approach corridors on the extended centrelines, and terminal sectors whose floors step up away from the arrival direction and over the high ground in this file. They carry derivation "approx". Aerodrome traffic zones are computed from a rule -- 2.5 NM where the longest runway is over 1850 m and 2 NM otherwise, to 2000 ft above the aerodrome -- and carry derivation "rule". The control zone and the terminal area outline are unchanged and still rule-derived. Everything else in the airspace block is CONSTRUCTED and comes from no AIP or sector file: approach corridors along the extended centrelines, which bring the base of controlled airspace down to 1500 ft outside the zone, and terminal sub-areas whose bases step up away from the arrival direction and over the high ground in this file. They carry derivation "approx". None of them encloses the aerodrome, so none of them joins the area of responsibility: that is still the control zone and the terminal area, exactly as before. Aerodrome traffic zones are computed from a rule -- 2.5 NM where the longest runway is over 1850 m and 2 NM otherwise, to 2000 ft above the aerodrome -- and carry derivation "rule".

challenge: Mountains take half the airspace, so every vector is over water and every base is short.
